papers.title: Representation-Aware Closed-Surface Parameterization: Exact Sensitivity Analysis and Pole-Aware Planar Preconditioning
papers.abstract: Surface parameterization is a fundamental task in geometry processing and shape analysis. For topologically closed surfaces, it is common to parameterize them onto a standardized closed domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with a prime example being a unit sphere for genus-0 closed surfaces. Many mapping methods use planar projections and perform computations on the plane rather than directly on the 3D surface. However, perturbations introduced before projection or geometric evolution propagate through the computation and may affect map quality, convergence, stopping behavior, and geometric validity. In this work, we formulate representation sensitivity as a branchwise input--output problem, separating smooth propagation through active Jacobians from changes in anchors, stopping rules, and fallback events. Under consistent piecewise-linear assembly, the unmodified south-pole Beltrami correction in the FLASH method for spherical conformal parameterization reduces exactly to source-mesh harmonic extension. On a fixed-anchor branch, the corrected map factors into chart transition, harmonic propagation, and inverse stereographic projection, yielding an explicit sensitivity Jacobian and a finite-triangle conditioning bound. Separately, we introduce a bounded five-parameter affine preconditioner over planar scale, translation, and anisotropy and evaluate candidates on the corrected spherical map. Across 30 genus-0 surfaces, it reduces median polar upper-tail log-condition and chord-angle distortion by $10.17\%$ and $10.97\%$, respectively, with both measures improving on every mesh. We also apply the framework to other spherical mapping methods including the conformalized mean-curvature flow and spherical density-equalizing maps. Altogether, our work highlights the importance of representation selection as a structural and practical component of spherical parameterization and downstream computation.

papers.title: DiffStent: Surrogate Adjoint Differentiation for Stent Deployment in Anisotropic Arteries
papers.abstract: We present DiffStent, a differentiable finite element framework for simulating arterial deformation during in silico stent deployment, where nearly incompressible, anisotropic vessel walls undergo large deformation and frictional contact with the stent. DiffStent combines the fiber-reinforced Holzapfel-Gasser-Ogden constitutive model with an implicit discrete adjoint that differentiates the converged mechanical equilibrium without unrolling the nonlinear solver, thus reducing the memory cost by three orders of magnitude. We identify three mechanisms that can lead to inaccurate, unstable, or uninformative gradients: nonsmooth switching, state mismatch, and gradient cancellation. To address these, we apply a contact surrogate in the backward pass while retaining the original physical model in the forward pass. We show superior gradient accuracy of our method over AutoDiff and finite differencing across constitutive benchmarks, idealized stented vessels, and patient-specific calcified coronary anatomies, and use the resulting sensitivities to quantify how tissue properties and calcification patterns govern lumen expansion and arterial wall stress. Finally, we demonstrate that DiffStent enables gradient-based system identification from retrospective clinical images of atherosclerotic coronary anatomy. Together, these results establish a practical approach for differentiating through nonlinear biomechanical simulations with stiff constitutive laws and nonsmooth contact, enabling patient-specific parameter inference and optimization in computational cardiovascular mechanics.

papers.title: The Rise of Low Precision Floating Point
papers.abstract: Floating point computing has dominated scientific computations since the 1950s because of its versatile ability to approximate real numbers with both sufficiently high precision and sufficiently great range. Since 1985, two specific formats have become standard across the industry, one with 32 bits which is adequate for many purposes and one with 64 bits which allows numbers with both much higher precision and much greater range for applications where these are needed. However, during the past decade, deep learning has come to dominate computation, and narrower floating point formats with lower precision and reduced range have steadily become more common. In this article we discuss this phenomenon, why it is happening, how various 16-bit, 8-bit and even 4-bit floating point formats have been developed, and efforts to standardize these formats.

papers.title: Learning to evolve by matching velocities
papers.abstract: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.

papers.title: A SPIDER-type stochastic subgradient method for expectation-constrained nonconvex nonsmooth optimization
papers.abstract: Many real-world problems, such as those with fairness constraints, involve complex expectation constraints and large datasets, necessitating the design of efficient stochastic methods to solve them. Most existing research focuses on cases with no {constraint} or easy-to-project constraints or deterministic constraints. In this paper, we consider nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization problems with expectation constraints, for which we build a novel exact penalty model. We first show the relationship between the penalty model and the original problem. Then on solving the penalty problem, we present a single-loop SPIDER-type stochastic subgradient method, which utilizes the subgradients of both the objective and constraint functions, as well as the constraint function value at each iteration. Under certain regularity conditions (weaker than Slater-type constraint qualification or strong feasibility assumed in existing works), we establish an iteration complexity result of $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ to reach a near-$\epsilon$ stationary point of the penalized problem in expectation, matching the lower bound for such tasks. Building on the exact penalization, an $(\epsilon,\epsilon)$-KKT point of the original problem is obtained. For a few scenarios, our complexity of either the {objective} sample subgradient or the constraint sample function values can be lower than the state-of-the-art results by a factor of $\epsilon^{-2}$. Moreover, on solving two fairness-constrained problems and a multi-class Neyman-Pearson classification problem, our method is significantly (up to 466 times) faster than the state-of-the-art algorithms, including switching subgradient method and inexact proximal point methods.

papers.title: Low-rank corrections to a shared reference Jacobian for GPU-parallel AC $N\!-\!1$ contingency analysis
papers.abstract: Contingency analysis repeatedly solves the power-flow equations under many single-element outages, an increasingly demanding workload as operating margins tighten and renewable variability grows. Graphics processing units (GPUs) are attractive for this task, but a change in topology alters the sparsity pattern of the Jacobian, preventing the uniform batched factorization on which efficient GPU solvers rely. This paper presents a GPU-parallel Newton--Raphson solver for $N\!-\!1$ contingency analysis that separates the change in operating state from the change in topology. A single reference Jacobian is inverted once and reused across all contingencies. Each topology change is expressed as a low-rank Woodbury correction, while the residual state-dependent perturbation is handled by an inner iterative solve, a truncated Neumann series or the biconjugate gradient stabilized method. We analyze the spectral radius and condition number of the resulting iteration matrices and show that the reference Jacobian is an effective preconditioner. On transmission-scale benchmarks, the method attains per-topology solve times competitive with an optimized 80-core central processing unit baseline, with the low-rank correction accounting for approximately 1--2\% of the workload. This makes GPU-parallel $N\!-\!1$ contingency analysis feasible at transmission scale without per-topology refactorization.

papers.title: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling
papers.abstract: GPU acceleration of finite element assembly is well established for standard formulations, but mixed-dimensional problems, in which volumetric subdomains are coupled via lower-dimensional interfaces, remain unsupported in automated frameworks such as FEniCS. We extend cuDOLFINx, a GPU-enabled extension of the DOLFINx finite element framework, to assemble such interface problems on GPUs while preserving the high-level FEniCS programming model. Combined with GPU-resident Krylov solvers and algebraic multigrid preconditioning, this enables end-to-end GPU execution of the EMI (Extracellular--Membrane--Intracellular) model, an elliptic interface problem from cardiac modeling in which many intracellular subdomains are coupled through membranes. We compare the GPU implementation against a CPU-based one through strong and weak scaling experiments on regular and realistic 3D cardiac geometries with up to 8000 cells and 22 million degrees of freedom. In terms of assembly, a single GH200 node is roughly equivalent to two 144-core CPU nodes in strong scaling, and to two to three nodes in weak scaling, depending on geometry. For the linear solver, performance depends on geometry, preconditioning, and problem scale. On the regular geometry, GPU advantages emerge mainly at larger problem sizes and node counts. On the realistic geometry, with the same algebraic multigrid preconditioner for both architectures, the GPU is faster at all tested scales. The implementation is available as open-source software and applies to other problems with interface coupling.

papers.title: Scaling global tractography with ExaTract: from large cohorts to ultra-high-resolution datasets
papers.abstract: Global tractography offers a theoretical framework for reconstructing white matter connectivity from diffusion MRI by jointly inferring all streamlines and their consistency with the diffusion signal and underlying anatomical priors. However, its sequential nature and log-linear complexity make it computationally prohibitive at the scales demanded by neuroimaging, from large population cohorts such as the Human Connectome Project (HCP) to ex vivo ultra-high-field acquisitions at mesoscopic resolution. In this work, we present ExaTract, a parallelized spin-glass tractography framework designed for high-performance computing (HPC) architectures. Implemented as an open-source MPI+Kokkos application, ExaTract partitions the tractography domain into spatially overlapping regions processed across distributed memory nodes, with regular synchronization of boundary modifications to preserve global convergence guarantees. We validate ExaTract on both in vivo and ex vivo diffusion MRI data: the complete HCP dataset demonstrates population-scale throughput, while the high-resolution Chenonceau dataset provides the first mesoscopic structural connectome derived from global tractography.

papers.title: Loss of Monotonicity in the Vector Play Model and Consequences for Newton-Type Solvers
papers.abstract: The vector play model (VPM) replaces the implicit minimization of the energy-based hysteresis model (EBM) by an explicit update. Its tangent contains the product of the Hessians of two unrelated potentials and is unsymmetric. Hence, the VPM has no co-energy density at frozen memory, and the skew part makes $\boldsymbol{H}\mapsto\boldsymbol{B}$ lose monotonicity in a band just outside the pinning circle, into which small time steps drive the sliding states. In composite models, the determinant of the tangent can change sign, which explains published failures of the local inversion $\boldsymbol{B}\mapsto\boldsymbol{H}$, and where it is negative, $\boldsymbol{H}\mapsto\boldsymbol{B}$ is not injective. In the scalar potential formulation, the exact tangent keeps a descent guarantee, whereas symmetric surrogates of the tangent, such as the symmetrized tangent or Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) updates, lose it and become ascent directions where the skew part dominates, as computations of TEAM Problem 32 confirm. It is therefore recommended to use solvers with an unsymmetric tangent.

papers.title: A Hierarchical direct solver for Lippmann-Schwinger equations based on boundary traces
papers.abstract: A high-order hierarchical direct solver for variable-media scattering in two dimensions is presented. Standard discretizations for these problems produce dense linear systems that are commonly solved iteratively, requiring a new global solve for each incident field. The method proposed here instead constructs a reusable scattering operator for the inhomogeneous medium, based on a hierarchical subdivision of the computational domain. First, high-accuracy leaf scattering operators are built from discretized local integral equations. Up the hierarchy, neighboring boxes are merged to build the scattering operators for successively larger boxes. A key feature of the method is that each scattering operator is represented as a map of incoming traces to outgoing traces. Consequently, volume unknowns appear only in the leaf computations; all higher levels of the hierarchy operate entirely on boundary traces. The hierarchical solver is presented first at the continuum level and discretized only afterward using high-order local volume quadrature, polynomial trace representations, and boundary integral techniques. For a discretization involving $N$ degrees of freedom, the method requires $O(N^{3/2})$ work and $O(N\log N)$ storage to build all scattering operators. Once these are available, any incoming field can be processed at cost $O(N)$ if only the outgoing field is required, and cost $O(N\log N)$ if the full field is required. Numerical experiments demonstrate high-order accuracy on a range of challenging scattering problems including cavities, back-scattering, limited regularity, and high wavenumber, that pose significant challenges to iterative methods.

papers.title: A comparison of parallel iterative methods for ILU triangular solves
papers.abstract: Exact triangular solves parallelise poorly, limited by the size and number of the level sets, so on GPUs the factors from incomplete LU (ILU) factorisations are often solved approximately with parallel iterative methods. We compare four such methods: a Jacobi method, an Incomplete Sparse Approximate Inverse (ISAI), GMRES polynomials, and AIRG, a reduction multigrid built on GMRES polynomials, for which we introduce a parallel coarse/fine splitting that bounds the diagonal dominance ratio of the fine-fine block. We test them with ILU(0) and ILU(1) factors of canonical PDE problems and 91 SuiteSparse/Matrix Market matrices, the latter on a single GPU. AIRG is the most robust on the PDE factors, with nearly flat iteration counts under refinement and no per-problem tuning, but has the largest setup and memory costs. GMRES polynomials are more robust than the Jacobi method at a similar cost. As the inner solve of an ILU preconditioner with tuned inner iteration counts, ISAI gives the largest median speedups over a hipSPARSE exact triangular solve (4.5$\times$ and 6.8$\times$ for ILU(0) and ILU(1)), though this was dominated by smaller problems; on the largest ILU(1) problems all four methods give similar median speedups of 2.1-2.6$\times$.

papers.title: Unconditional optimal convergence of a relaxation Crank-Nicolson difference scheme for 2D space-fractional NLS
papers.abstract: In this paper, we develop a linearly implicit relaxation Crank-Nicolson difference scheme for the two-dimensional space-fractional nonlinear Schr\"odinger (SFNS) equation, where the fractional Laplacian is approximated by a simple fractional central difference scheme. The proposed scheme is uniquely solvable and conserves discrete mass for general real-valued nonlinear coefficients, and a modified discrete energy in the cubic case. By introducing a modified error system employing a cut-off technique, we establish the optimal-order error estimates without mesh-ratio restriction. Specifically, the primary variable achieves second-order temporal and spatial convergence in the discrete $H_h^{\alpha/2}$-norm, and the relaxation variable satisfies the same convergence in the discrete $L^2$-norm. Some numerical experiments confirm the relevant theoretical results.

papers.title: Parameter Bounds and Inverse Approximation for Linearized ReLU$^k$ Networks on the Sphere
papers.abstract: We study direct and inverse approximation for linearized shallow ReLU$^k$ networks on $\mathbb S^d$ with quasi-uniform hidden parameters. For $0<\alpha<\frac{d+2k+1}{2d}$, under the coefficient growth condition $\bigl(n\sum_{j=1}^na_{j,n}^2\bigr)^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq n^\alpha M$, we prove that approximation at the order $n^{-\frac{d+2k+1}{2d}+\alpha}$ is equivalent to membership in the parity-compatible Besov space $\mathcal B_{2,\infty,*}^{\frac{d+2k+1}{2}-\alpha d}(\mathbb S^d)$. Mere convergence under the same coefficient budget does not imply this regularity. For unconstrained approximation along a nested parameter sequence, a single ridge function gives a counterexample when $\alpha<\frac{1}{2}$, whereas for $\alpha>\frac{1}{2}$ the endpoint Besov inverse conclusion follows from a Bernstein inequality under antipodal quasi-uniformity. The inverse conclusion is also recovered when the prescribed rate holds for two quasi-uniform parameter sequences whose union is antipodally separated.

papers.title: A posteriori error estimates for a finite volume approximation of a local sensing Keller-Segel model
papers.abstract: A local sensing Keller-Segel model, in which cells adjust their motility to the local chemoattractant rather than its gradient, and a semi-implicit finite volume scheme for its numerical approximation are studied. Computable a posteriori bounds for the approximation error measured in terms of the $L^\infty(0, T; H^{-1}(\Omega))$ and $L^2(0, T; L^2(\Omega))$ norms of the cell density are derived based on a new stability estimate and suitable reconstructions of the flux and the flux potential of the numerical solution. Optimal scaling of the estimates is numerically demonstrated in 1D and 2D experiments. Moreover, an adaptive mesh refinement method steered by the estimator is proposed for the 1D case, and its efficiency is numerically verified.

papers.title: Flux vector splittings and semi-implicit finite volume schemes for an isentropic two-phase flow model
papers.abstract: We present two new semi-implicit finite volume schemes for the 1D hyperbolic and thermodynamically compatible (HTC) isentropic two-phase flow model of Romenski et al., written in terms of mixture density, volume fraction, partial gas density, mixture momentum and the relative phase velocity. In gas-liquid mixtures, the sound speed of the weakly compressible liquid is much larger than the gas sound speed and flow velocity, so the time step of fully explicit discretizations is dictated by liquid acoustic waves, even when the interest lies in the dynamics of the gas. To overcome this difficulty, the model's flux is split at the continuous level into an explicit subsystem (gas dynamics) and an implicit subsystem (liquid acoustic waves), leading to a nonlinear system for liquid pressure solved with the Newton method. In the first splitting the entire liquid phase is treated implicitly, while in the second the liquid convective terms are moved to the explicit subsystem, so only liquid acoustic waves are treated implicitly and nested Picard iterations are avoided. Thus, the time step of both schemes is restricted only by flow velocities and gas sound speed, independent of liquid sound speed. We prove and numerically confirm that both schemes exactly preserve the Abgrall condition (uniform velocity and pressure across material interfaces). For well-prepared initial data, both schemes are consistent with the volume balance of the liquid's low Mach number limit. Riemann problems, pressure equilibrium tests and acoustic tests show that in non-stiff regimes the semi-implicit schemes reproduce the results of a fully explicit scheme, while in the stiff regime they allow time steps that are up to 3-4 orders of magnitude larger, avoiding the excessive numerical dissipation of explicit schemes whose numerical viscosity is dictated by liquid sound speed.

papers.title: A Second-Order Stochastic Dynamic Mode Decomposition by Richardson Extrapolation
papers.abstract: Stochastic dynamic mode decomposition (SDMD) approximates the Koopman semigroup of an It\^o diffusion by a Galerkin generator matrix on a dictionary of observables, computed from samples of the invariant law and evaluations of the generator, and advances observables with a first-order stochastic Taylor step (SDMD-1). The second-order Taylor step (SDMD-2) also needs the matrix of second generator actions, hence a dictionary with four derivatives, evaluations of a fourth-order differential operator at every sample, and a third matrix. We show that the Richardson extrapolation of two SDMD-1 half steps (SDMD-R) is second-order accurate with the data, the matrices, and the regularity of SDMD-1. One error bound covers exact and empirical Galerkin matrices. It consists of the Galerkin error of the dictionary, which is common to all schemes, a time-stepping term, and a data term of order $m^{-1/2}$ in the sample size $m$. The time-stepping term is $O(\dt^2)$ for SDMD-R and $O(\Theta_N\dt+\dt^2)$ for SDMD-2, where $\Theta_N$ is the norm of the second-order Galerkin residual $\Proj_N\cA(I-\Proj_N)\cA|_{\cV_N}$. The first-order term is attained and, for self-adjoint generators, vanishes only for generator-invariant dictionaries. For reversible periodic diffusions and trigonometric dictionaries with cutoff $K$, the step restriction $\dt\lesssim K^{-2}$ makes all three schemes contractions, and the error against the Koopman semigroup on $H^\ell$ observables is $O(K^{-(\ell-2)}+\dt^p)$ plus a sampling term of order $K^{d+2}m^{-1/2}$ in dimension $d$, with $p=1$ for SDMD-1 and $p=2$ for SDMD-R and SDMD-2. Numerical experiments confirm that SDMD-R matches or improves on the accuracy of SDMD-2 at the cost of SDMD-1.

papers.title: Efficient second-order physics-preserving schemes for incompressible flows with variable density and viscosity
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel second-order prediction--filter--projection framework for incompressible flows with variable density and viscosity. In this framework, a constrained $L^2$-projection is enforced to unconditionally preserve the prescribed density bounds and discrete mass conservation, while a generalized-Laplacian reformulation combined with the D-CSAV approach is used to discretize the variable-viscosity momentum equation. In particular, a density-weighted second-order time filter is proposed, which eliminates the additional uniform-in-time bound restriction imposed on the time difference quotient of the discrete density in existing stability analyses. The resulting scheme is shown to satisfy an unconditional modified-energy dissipation law, without the viscosity-related restrictions imposed in earlier work. Then, an additional scalar auxiliary variable and its compatible temporal discretization are introduced to construct a variable-step prediction--filter--projection scheme. This scheme is also bound-preserving and mass-conserving, and satisfies an unconditional modified-energy dissipation law. Moreover, the modified energy is much closer to the ``original'' kinetic energy, differing from it only through the auxiliary-variable corrections. Based on the variable-step scheme, a reliable energy-based adaptive time-stepping strategy is developed. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, physics-preserving properties, and efficiency of the proposed schemes.

papers.title: A structure-preserving finite volume scheme for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation with nondegenerate state-dependent mobility
papers.abstract: We construct and analyze a fully discrete finite volume scheme for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation with nondegenerate state-dependent mobility. The scheme combines a standard two-point flux approximation of diffusion, the L1 approximation of the Caputo derivative on a uniform time grid, and a semiconvex splitting of the potential, and it discretizes the inverse mobility by a secant average multiplying the entire L1 derivative. The key estimate is a lower bound for the accumulated pairing of this weighted L1 derivative with the solution increments in terms of the accumulated L1 quadratic form. Using this lower bound, we derive a discrete energy estimate and the time regularity required for compactness. For twice continuously differentiable semiconvex potentials satisfying sign conditions outside $(-1,1)$ and initial data in $H^1(\Omega)$ taking values in $[-1,1]$, we prove existence of at least one fully discrete solution on every admissible finite volume mesh and every uniform time grid. Every such solution satisfies the maximum bound principle and a discrete energy bound relative to the initial energy, without a time-step restriction. In up to three space dimensions, under a mesh regularity condition with a constant independent of the mesh size, we prove that any sequence of fully discrete solutions has a subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(\Omega\times(0,T))$ to a weak solution of the continuous problem as the mesh size and time step tend to zero. As a consequence, we obtain existence of a weak solution in one and two space dimensions, and in three dimensions whenever such meshes exist.

papers.title: A Clustered Equivalent-Source Method with Local Response Compression and Group-Symmetry Reduction for Antenna-Array Analysis
papers.abstract: Full-wave analysis of finite antenna arrays is computationally demanding because detailed element responses must be resolved and coupled across the entire array. To reduce this cost, this paper presents a clustered equivalent-source method that combines local response compression with group-symmetry reduction. Local responses are represented in compressed equivalent-surface bases or coordinates inherited from child clusters. Symmetry constraints associated with the cluster partition and excitation reduce the coupled system, while the corresponding group transformations recover the complete response in the retained coordinates. To assess overall efficiency, we evaluate the costs of local construction, propagation, global solution, and recovery. Numerical examples involving layered and finite annular patch arrays show close agreement between the computed and reference complex far fields and shorter complete-run times than those of the corresponding symmetry-reduced direct solvers. Among the three equivalent-source implementations for the layered array, the one with the smallest coupled system has the longest runtime because local construction and propagation dominate the cost. These findings highlight the need to consider local construction and coupling costs when assessing the benefit of reducing the global system dimension.

papers.title: Closed-Form Gaussian Mixture Representations of d-Dimensional Triangulated Domains
papers.abstract: We derive a Gaussian Mixture (GM) representation of a full-dimensional subset of Euclidean space with finite volume from a finite simplicial triangulation in closed form. On each simplex, we replace the uniform probability density function (PDF) with a Gaussian PDF that minimizes the Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence, arriving at the information projection onto the family of Gaussian PDFs. By exploiting affine isomorphisms between simplices, the joint convexity and bijection invariance properties of the KL divergence, identities for Dirichlet PDFs, and a partition-of-unity argument, we establish a dimension-dependent but geometry-independent sharp upper bound on the global KL divergence between the resulting GM PDF and the uniform PDF on the original domain. Numerical examples illustrate the construction and demonstrate its potential in practical applications.

papers.title: Alternative Tikhonov-Type Regularization for the Calder\'on Inverse Conductivity Problem
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the application of two regularization methods, classical Tikhonov and Alternative Tikhonov regularization, to the Calder\'on inverse conductivity problem. We develop an iterative reconstruction scheme based on linearizing the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map and approximating conductivity updates using Gaussian basis functions. The resulting linear systems are solved using both regularization methods, with particular attention given to the derivation and numerical implementation of Alternative Tikhonov regularization. We compare the performance of these methods through numerical experiments on a synthetic conductivity containing two localized regions of differing conductivity. A total of 666 reconstruction tests are performed across varying regularization parameters, damping factors, and iteration counts. The lowest relative reconstruction errors obtained are 0.064730 for Alternative Tikhonov and 0.065173 for classical Tikhonov regularization. Although both methods produce comparable reconstructions, Alternative Tikhonov achieves the lowest observed error. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of both approaches within the proposed reconstruction scheme and motivate further investigation into parameter selection, numerical stability, and reconstruction accuracy.

papers.title: Massively parallel Schwarz methods for the high-frequency Helmholtz equation with O(k) convergence
papers.abstract: We develop a one-level restricted additive Schwarz solver with perfectly matched layer transmission conditions (RAS--PML) for high-frequency Helmholtz systems. For problems with ${O}(k^d)$ unknowns, $d=2,3$, the solver uses Cartesian decompositions and ${O}(k^d)$ concurrent local solves for a single right-hand side, where $k$ is the wavenumber. Starting from the convergence theory for fixed decompositions established in~\texttt{arXiv:2404.02156}, we address the growing cost {as $k$ increases} of local solves through a nested RAS--PML construction. Under suitable stability and contraction assumptions, we prove that sufficiently accurate recursive local solves preserve convergence of the outer iteration. We also prove that a single inner iteration at each non-terminal level yields a correction algebraically equivalent to one-level RAS--PML, provided that the hierarchy-induced finest local problems and composite restriction and weighted extension operators are retained. This equivalence provides a hierarchical interpretation and permits a direct implementation without recursive transfers. We assess the one-level solver using PML and overlap widths of order ${O}(k^{-1}\log k)$. Constant-coefficient experiments cover $300\leq k\leq19200$ in two dimensions and $60\leq k\leq780$ in three dimensions, reaching $1.47\times10^9$ and $4.75\times10^8$ complex unknowns, respectively. Richardson iteration counts grow approximately linearly with $k$ over these ranges, while total parallel runtime, including setup and solution, exhibits near-linear growth at the larger tested wavenumbers. Further experiments assess the effects of mesh refinement and heterogeneous media.

papers.title: Minimum-Norm Interpolation in Weighted Variation Spaces: Direct and Inverse Problems
papers.abstract: We study minimum-norm interpolation in weighted variation spaces generated by ReLU$^s$ ridge functions on the unit ball, where $s$ is a positive integer. For a target $f$ in the weighted variation space and a node set with sufficiently small fill distance $h$, every minimum-norm interpolant satisfies the direct bound $\|f-\mathscr{I}_{X_h}f\|_{L_2(\mathbb{B}^d)}\lesssim_{d,s}h^{(2s+1)/4}\|f\|_{\mathcal{V}_s}$. Under a boundary separation condition on the nodes, we construct a matching lower bound for the worst-case interpolation error. For the inverse problem, we introduce dual certificates and derive an estimate analogous to a Bernstein inequality. Under suitable upper bounds on dictionary size and spectral lower bounds for the atomic Gram matrices, sufficiently fast $L_2$ convergence of minimum-norm interpolants along geometrically decreasing fill distances implies that the target belongs to $\mathcal{V}_s$. As a byproduct, the best $L_2$ approximation error $E_n(f)_{L_2(\mathbb{B}^d)}$ for shallow ReLU$^s$ networks of width at most $n$ satisfies $E_n(f)_{L_2(\mathbb{B}^d)}\lesssim_{d,s}n^{-1/2-(2s+1)/(2d)}\|f\|_{\mathcal{V}_s}$, with the weighted atomic cost of an approximating network bounded by a constant multiple of $\|f\|_{\mathcal{V}_s}$, independently of $n$.

papers.title: An Incidence-Based Edge-Averaged Method for Convection-Diffusion Problems on Polytopal Meshes
papers.abstract: We develop an incidence-based edge-averaged method for scalar convection-diffusion problems on convex polytopal meshes in arbitrary dimensions. The proposed method extends the classical edge-averaged finite-element scheme through a graph-theoretic formulation based on vertex-edge incidence matrices. We first establish this formulation on simplices in arbitrary dimensions and then extend it to convex polytopes by introducing complementary edges and generalized barycentric coordinates. A key ingredient is a matrix identity that relates the generalized Whitney edge mass matrix to a diagonal representation of the Poisson stiffness matrix, enabling an exponentially-fitted discretization expressed entirely in terms of nodal values and edge weights. We prove that the resulting stiffness matrix is a nonsingular $M$-matrix under suitable positivity and connectivity conditions, ensuring monotonicity and the discrete maximum principle. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional simplicial and nonsimplicial meshes demonstrate first-order convergence in the $H^1$ semi-norm and stable, nonoscillatory solutions in convection-dominated regimes.

papers.title: Online Autotuning of Algebraic Multigrid via Contextual Bandits and Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Algebraic multigrid (AMG) methods are widely used for solving large sparse linear systems, but their efficiency depends strongly on interacting setup and solve parameters. Effective parameter choices typically depend on the problem. We develop a phase-aware online autotuning method for hypre's BoomerAMG to reduce cumulative time-to-solution over sequences of related linear systems. A LinUCB-based contextual bandit selects mixed-type parameters for AMG hierarchy construction using a shared cost model over PDE descriptors and configuration encodings. A recursive LSTDQ controller uses residual and timing observations to estimate the AMG solve time within each attempt and adapt relaxation weights between multigrid cycles. Both learners update from ongoing solves without offline pretraining. Across grids of sizes $40^3$, $60^3$, and $80^3$, the joint autotuning method reduces total runtime, including recurring learner computation, by 36.1-43.3% for diffusion problems and 19.8-31.0% for diffusion-advection problems over sequences of 5000 linear systems, relative to the reference BoomerAMG default configuration. On a variable-flow diffusion-advection benchmark comprising 30,000 systems on a $60^3$ grid, 2 systems fail to converge with joint autotuning, compared with 1677 for the reference configuration, under their respective attempt budgets.

papers.title: Accelerating posterior sampling in Bayesian inverse problems with diffusion models: an online-offline perspective
papers.abstract: Bayesian inverse problems require both informative prior models and computationally feasible posterior inference. Score-based diffusion models provide expressive learned priors, but their use for inversion introduces a conditioning problem: the score of a noised posterior is generally unavailable from a prior score alone. This selective survey reviews the principal approaches to that problem, including likelihood guidance, spectral and projection methods, sequential Monte Carlo corrections, and amortized conditional training. We organize methods by how they split cost between offline preparation and online inference, and compare their assumptions, advantages and limitations, with emphasis on computational speedups. Some ongoing directions and open questions are gathered at the end.

papers.title: Fully Discrete Error Analysis of the CSLDG Scheme with Numerical Characteristic Tracing and Spline Reconstruction
papers.abstract: A semi-Lagrangian discontinuous finite element scheme based on the characteristic Galerkin method (CSLDG) is investigated.The scheme directly discretizes an integral invariant model derived from the coupling of the transport equation and its adjoint equation.we have established, for the first time, error estimates for the fully discrete CSLDG scheme over a general domain \Omega in \mathbb{R}^d.The error is decomposed into three parts: the ideal numerical solution error (the difference between the exact solution and the spatial discretization), the time-dependent test function error (the deviation of the test function caused by the numerical characteristic backtracking via an ODE solver), and the upstream region approximation error (the integration region deviation induced by numerical characteristic backtracking and spline boundary reconstruction).Under either compact-support boundary conditions or periodic boundary conditions with the velocity field and the solution sharing the same spatial periodicity, without requiring incompressibility,and assuming the standard CFL condition (\Delta t=O(h)) linking the time step and the mesh size, the following results are proved:Using piecewise P^K polynomial spaces, the L^2 error of the ideal numerical solution attains a suboptimal order O(h^K); If the ODE solver order satisfies D \ge 2K+2+d, the overall error retains the suboptimal order even after incorporating the time-dependent test function error;When the upstream region approximation error is further taken into account, for d \ge 2 the overall error remains suboptimal O(h^K) provided the spline reconstruction degree satisfies r \ge \max(K+1+d, d+2);

papers.title: Robust preconditioners for finite element approximations of control-state constrained optimal control problems governed by elliptic equations
papers.abstract: The goal of this paper is to derive robust preconditioners for integral control-state constrained optimal control problems governed by the second order partial differential equations with linear finite element approximations. We give corresponding discretized systems of the first order necessary and sufficient optimality conditions, and get six linear algebraic systems with saddle point schemes. Furthermore, we propose efficient block preconditioners to solve the corresponding linearized algebraic systems. With respect to both mesh sizes and inherent parameters, the robustness of proposed preconditioners is proved with explicit eigenvalues of minimal polynomials. Meanwhile, we design two algorithms and choose the incomplete $LU$ factorizations to deduce the computations. Two numerical experiments are given to depict the efficiency of our proposed preconditioners.

papers.title: Rank-Optimal Sample Complexity of Riemannian Gauss-Newton for Low-Rank Matrix Recovery
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the recovery of an unknown rank-$r$ matrix $\boldsymbol{X}_\star \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times n_2}$ from Gaussian linear measurements using the Riemannian Gauss-Newton (RGN) algorithm. Each iteration of RGN solves the RGN equation followed by a fixed-rank retraction. We prove that, with high probability, RGN with spectral initialization converges quadratically to $\boldsymbol{X}_\star$ using $\mathcal{O} ( r(n_1+n_2)\kappa^2 )$ measurements, where $\kappa$ is the condition number of $\boldsymbol{X}_\star$. This is the first result to simultaneously achieve rank-optimal sample complexity and quadratic convergence for Gaussian low-rank matrix sensing. The key to the proof is a sharp spectral-norm analysis of the iterates, which requires controlling the inverse operator arising from the RGN equation. Our analysis develops an exact finite Neumann expansion of this inverse operator and combines it with a virtual-sequence decoupling argument and the restricted isometry property. Extensive numerical experiments support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the advantages of RGN.

papers.title: Energy-Dissipative, High-Order BDF Schemes for Simulating Geometric Flows via Energy Increments
papers.abstract: We propose energy-dissipative backward differentiation formula (BDF) methods for geometric flows in the Barrett--Garcke--N\"urnberg (BGN) parametric finite element framework. Starting from a Lagrange-multiplier formulation, we replace the multistep approximation of the energy derivative by an energy-increment equation while retaining the BDF geometric equations. The Simpson quadrature and two interleaved time grids provide third- and fourth-order constructions. The positive quadrature weights ensure stepwise decay of the original discrete geometric energy for every nondegenerate solution of the nonlinear system. We establish an explicit conditional consistency bound for the scalar energy equation and a regularity criterion for the Newton system of curve-shortening flows. Then, the proposed schemes extend to simulating curve diffusion, mean curvature flow, and surface diffusion. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate geometric accuracy, energy decay, good mesh distribution, and high performance of the proposed schemes.
